## What we covered

We finished the two slides left over from the hospital-price class, price
transparency and competition, and then started on pricing itself. A hospital
that sets its own price, a hospital that takes the price it's given, and the
beginning of the case where it faces both at once.

## Key points

- Price transparency is harder than it sounds. A vet can post a chart on the
  wall because the service is known in advance and the price is the same for
  everyone. In an emergency department neither holds. Nobody knows yet which of
  twenty things is wrong with you, finding out is most of what gets billed, and
  the price depends on who your insurer is. Even with a good posted price, you
  usually don't know what treatment you need, a lot of care isn't planned, your
  network limits where you can go, and a cheaper hospital you have to reach by
  ambulance isn't cheaper. For an uninsured patient, a posted price that's
  already out of reach can mean not going at all.
- Posted prices can push prices up, and the mechanism is the bargaining model
  we already have. If I can see that you're paying the hospital across town more
  than you're paying me for the same service, I ask for that number in the next
  negotiation, and no coordination between hospitals is needed. What would push
  the other way is patients using the information to shop, and there are good
  reasons to doubt that, since insurance absorbs most of the difference and much
  of the decision isn't yours anyway. Economists made this argument before the
  rule took effect, and the clearest precedent, posted prices in the Danish
  concrete market, saw prices rise.
- How the rule was written mattered as much as the rule itself. Hospitals have
  to post a machine-readable file and a consumer-friendly one, and what they
  produced was thousands of unlabeled codes spread across spreadsheets and JSON
  files. Some posted nothing for well over a year before any fine arrived.
  Compliance is
  better now and still incomplete, and the files are messy enough that companies
  exist to scrape them, clean them, and sell the result.
- A student asked about price ceilings. They come up for prescription drugs and
  rarely for hospital or physician services, because there's no mechanism to
  impose one on a commercial contract. Medicare and Medicaid fix their prices,
  so those work as both a ceiling and a floor, but nothing requires a commercial
  price to stay below some level.
- More competition usually lowers prices, but not always. If patients respond to
  quality much more than to price, hospitals compete on quality, quality costs
  money, and prices can rise. That doesn't make competition beside the point
  here. We allocate health care through a market and then don't give that market
  much competition to work with. The Guardian article on Parkview Health in
  Fort Wayne, linked on the slides, is the case study. One system bought up
  hospitals and physician practices around it and kept raising prices, with no
  competitive force pushing them down. A hospital still has to bargain with
  insurers, but when it's the only one in town the insurers don't have much
  recourse.
- We don't need a separate model for not-for-profits. You can write one down,
  utility over profit from private payers, profit from public payers, and the
  amount of care delivered, but without knowing the weight on each piece it
  predicts nothing, so we assume profit maximization for everyone. A hospital
  with price-setting power is then the firm you already know. My advice is to
  write out the profit function and differentiate it rather than memorizing
  marginal revenue. You won't always be able to see what marginal revenue is,
  and the derivative always works. The example we did is on the slides, and the
  second one is on the website for you to work. Marginal revenue falls faster
  than demand because selling one more unit means lowering the price for every
  buyer rather than only the marginal one. If you could price-discriminate
  perfectly, the two would be the same line.
- A pure price taker has a flat marginal revenue curve. An outside payer has
  fixed what you get for the next unit of care, so only your cost curve shapes
  the decision. That isn't capitation. Under capitation revenue is fixed in
  total and each additional unit of care lowers profit.
- Put the two together and marginal revenue has a kink. Picture two lines of
  patients at the door, one commercial and one Medicare, and take them in order
  of marginal revenue. Commercial patients start above the Medicare price, so
  you serve them first, and once commercial marginal revenue has fallen to the
  Medicare price you switch lines. Total quantity is still where marginal
  revenue meets marginal cost, but you have to know which branch you're on,
  which makes this a logic problem on top of a derivative problem. The private
  quantity is where the two marginal revenue curves meet, the rest up to the
  total is the public quantity, and the private price comes from the demand
  curve at the private quantity rather than at the total. Now cut the Medicare
  price. The kink moves right, the private quantity rises, and the private price
  falls. A Medicare patient is worth less to you than before, you'd rather fill
  that slot with a commercial patient, and the only way to attract one more
  commercial patient is to charge less. That's the opposite of cost shifting,
  the hospital industry's claim that Medicare cuts force commercial prices up.
  Cost shifting is also a different thing from cross-subsidization, which is
  funding a money-losing service out of a profitable one. That happens all the
  time and isn't controversial.
